newsitem.title: ITALY: Berlusconi trial judge rejects bias allegation.
newsitem.headline: Berlusconi trial judge rejects bias allegation.

text.p: The judge hearing the trial of former Italian prime minister Silvio Berlusconi on corruption charges rejected allegations of bias on Monday and said he would continue to hear the case.
"I do not intend to abstain from the proceedings. The session will continue with questioning of the defendants," judge Carlo Crivelli told the court in Milan.
He was responding to a formal challenge to his impartiality from media mogul Berlusconi, who has asked the Court of Appeal to dismiss Crivelli from the bench.
Berlusconi's younger brother and co-defendant, Paolo, and two other accused have lodged similar suits. They must be heard by the Court of Appeal although no date has been set.

Crivelli's announcement means the trial will go ahead pending an appeal court ruling. If Berlusconi's bid to oust the judge is admitted, the trial, which began on January 17, would have to restart from scratch.

Berlusconi, who denies charges of complicity in the payment of alleged bribes to tax officials by four companies in his Fininvest business empire, alleged at the weekend that Crivelli was actively siding with the prosecution.

He based his suit on a private exchange in court between Crivelli and prosecutor Gherardo Colombo in which Crivelli spoke of a "carrot and stick". The conversation, outside formal proceedings, was picked up on court microphones and transcribed.

Crivelli told the court on Monday that his remarks had been a reminder to Colombo, one of the stars of Milan's elite "Clean Hands" pool of anti-graft investigators, that he intended to strike a balance between prosecution and defence.
"Given that I have never expressed an opinion about any of the accused...I do not intend to abstain from the trial," he said.

Berlusconi, prime minister for seven months in 1994, is accused of having conspired in the payment to tax officers of alleged bribes totalling 380 million lire ($250,000) by four of his companies for lenient audits or other concessions between 1989 and 1981.

Still leader of the opposition centre-right Freedom Alliance, he has denied knowledge of the payments at the time they were made and argues that they were extorted. He also alleges the case is part of a political plot to ruin him.
Berlusconi attended the trial's opening in January but, in common with many of his co-defendants, has since exercised his right under Italian law not to be present in court.
His lawyer, Ennio Amodio, said on Monday that Crivelli's recorded remarks cast serious doubt on his impartiality and now would have to be scrutinised by the Court of Appeal.
"The facts speak for themselves," Amodio told reporters.
"There are two possibilities. Either remove the judge or restart the trial," he said.
